nameStory: The 'hooked' in hooked buttercup comes from the tiny curved hooks found on its seeds, which help them catch onto fur, feathers, and clothing for a free ride to new locations. It's also called 'blisterwort' because like other buttercups, the sap can cause skin irritation and blisters if you handle it too much.
description: Hooked buttercup is a modest woodland wildflower that stands about 1-2 feet tall in the dappled shade of New England's deciduous forests. Unlike its flashy meadow cousins, this buttercup has small, pale yellow flowers that seem almost shy among its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves. The whole plant has a soft, hairy texture and prefers to bloom in late spring before the forest canopy fully leafs out.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale yellow flowers, much smaller and less showy than other buttercups, with 5 small petals that are often shorter than the green sepals beneath them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palm-shaped leaves divided into 3-5 main lobes that are further subdivided, creating a lacy appearance; feel soft and slightly fuzzy on top

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect stems covered in long, soft hairs that you can easily feel when you brush against them; stands 1-2 feet tall without sprawling

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small seeds with tiny curved hooks that will stick to your clothes or pet's fur if you brush against mature seed heads

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Light green, round stems densely covered with long white hairs that give them a fuzzy, soft texture when touched

habitat: Look for hooked buttercup in moist, rich soils of deciduous woodlands throughout New England, especially in areas that stay damp but not waterlogged. It thrives in the dappled shade under maples, oaks, and other hardwood trees, often growing alongside other spring woodland flowers like trout lily and wild ginger.

seasonality.spring: Blooms in late spring (May-June) with small pale yellow flowers appearing before or just as the forest canopy fills in. This is the best time to spot its modest flowers.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and seed heads develop with their characteristic hooked seeds. Leaves remain green and visible but plants become less conspicuous in the summer shade.
seasonality.fall: Seeds are ripe and ready to hitchhike on passing animals. Leaves may turn yellow before dying back, and plants begin preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no visible trace above ground until the following spring.

funFact: While most buttercups are sun-lovers that blanket meadows in bright yellow, hooked buttercup is the introvert of the family—it actually prefers the cool, dim understory of forests and has evolved much smaller, paler flowers since it doesn't need to compete for pollinators' attention in the busy meadow marketplace.
confusionNotes: Its small, pale flowers and woodland habitat make it easy to distinguish from the bright, showy buttercups of fields and meadows. Remember: if you're in the woods and see a 'weak' yellow buttercup with deeply divided leaves, you've likely found the hooked buttercup.
contextualKnowledge: Like other members of the buttercup family, hooked buttercup contains compounds that can irritate skin and are toxic if eaten, so it's best admired from a respectful distance. The 'crowfoot' alternate name refers to the resemblance of the deeply divided leaves to a bird's foot.
compareHints: Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms. Small-flowered buttercup also has small flowers but grows in different habitats and has less deeply divided leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
